timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: When I delete a file, it's gone forever, right?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Absolutely not. The file system just marks the space as available. The data remains until overwritten.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: So someone could recover my old files?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: On an HDD, trivially. On an SSD, it's harder because of wear leveling, but not impossible.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: SSDs distribute writes evenly across memory cells to prevent burnout. The OS thinks a block is deleted, but the SSD moved it elsewhere.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: So how do you actually destroy data on an SSD?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: ATA Secure Erase command or full-disk encryption with key destruction. Simple overwriting won't cut it.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: What about encryption? Does that solve everything?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: BitLocker and LUKS encrypt data at rest, but if the key is stored on the same drive, you need to destroy the key to render data unreadable.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: So formatting a drive before selling it is basically useless?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Quick format? Absolutely useless. Full format with verification? Better, but still not guaranteed on SSDs.
